title: The throne of the timeless
hookLine: he raises a platform facing the Harmandir, where the community meets on worldly matters

cards: In the world Guru Hargobind grew up in, one throne counted: the emperor's. He sat high, and his word was law. Under him, governors sat on smaller thrones, and so on down; everyone knew who was above them.
Now the young Guru, wearing his two swords, does something bold. Right across from the Harmandir Sahib, facing its door, he builds a raised platform.
A seat where he holds court, receives visitors, hears disputes and talks over the community's worldly affairs. And he gives it a name that answers the question of whose throne counts.

teach.b: Takht means throne. Akal means timeless, beyond death, beyond time; you met it in the Mool Mantar: Akal Moorat, the timeless form. So the Akal Takht is the throne of the Timeless One, God's own throne.
Not the Guru's, and certainly not any emperor's.

teach.h: BUILT BY THE GURU AND HIS SIKHS.
teach.b: Sikh tradition says the Guru built it in 1606 with Baba Buddha and Bhai Gurdas, and no hired laborers, just the Guru and his Sikhs. Look at where it stands, because the placement is the teaching.

The Harmandir sits low in the middle of the pool, the house of the Name, of singing and remembering: piri. The Akal Takht faces it, where the community meets about worldly matters, justice, defense, decisions: miri.
Two buildings looking at each other, the spirit and the world in conversation, each keeping the other honest.
Tradition says that at the Harmandir the Guru would listen to hymns, and at the Takht he would sit as a leader, hear news, and review his horsemen.
The Akal Takht still stands, and still matters. Sikhs count it first among the five takhts, the seats of authority in Sikh life, and from there decisions are announced to Sikhs everywhere.
Its name makes a quiet claim: no earthly throne is final. Only the timeless one.

how: The Akal Takht in Amritsar is the foremost of the five takhts, the seats of Sikh temporal authority, and decisions and edicts for the Sikh community are issued from there.

o: the Guru's royal throne in Amritsar
the hall where the Mughal emperor sat
the throne of the Timeless One, God's throne

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the house of the Name: piri

s: the Akal Takht is the Guru's personal throne
it is the throne of the Timeless One, God's throne, not any person's.
it stands facing the Harmandir Sahib
the two buildings face each other: the spirit and the world in conversation.
tradition says hired laborers built it
tradition says the Guru, Baba Buddha and Bhai Gurdas built it with the Sikhs, no hired hands.

games.q: you're Guru Hargobind, building a seat to hold court. what do you name it?
games.why: he called it the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One: a claim that no earthly throne is final.

practice: If you can, go to a window or step outside, and look up for a few breaths: the sky, the clouds, whatever was here long before you.

Then look down at the ground, your feet, the place where your life actually happens; up again, down again, the two in conversation like the buildings facing each other across the path. Then settle, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Akal Takht. The throne of the Timeless One, built by Guru Hargobind facing the Harmandir Sahib, still the first seat of Sikh authority.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: akal, timeless; takht, throne (from Persian).

carryVoice: Your line: the timeless throne. No boss, bill or deadline gets to sit on it. That's day sixty-six.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on the founding of the Akal Takht (Akal Bunga) by Guru Hargobind, 1606
